Tutorial 9: Epidemiological Modeling (DLNM and Attributable Burden)

climasus4r Team

13/09/2026

Source: vignettes/09-modelagem.Rmd
09-modelagem.Rmd

Objective

By the end of this tutorial you will be able to turn a daily health series aligned with climate into epidemiological inference: estimate the non-linear and lagged relationship between temperature and mortality with a DLNM (sus_mod_dlnm()), quantify the attributable burden of heat and cold (sus_mod_af()), and get to know the other tools in climasus4r’s biostatistical toolkit — interrupted time series (sus_mod_its()), case-crossover (sus_mod_casecrossover()), and multi-city meta-analysis (sus_mod_pool()).

Modeling is the last stage of the pipeline. It consumes the output of the previous stages (the aggregated health series from Tutorial 4 and the aligned climate exposure from Tutorials 7 and 8) and produces relative risk estimates, attributable fractions, and publication-ready visualizations.

Scientific context

Modern environmental epidemiology treats the association between an environmental exposure (temperature, pollutants) and a daily count outcome (deaths, hospitalizations) as a problem that is both non-linear and lagged in time. Extreme heat kills on the same day or within 1–2 days (acute effect); cold kills over one to two weeks (delayed, prolonged effect). Modeling only the day’s temperature underestimates the effect of cold.

The Distributed Lag Non-linear Model (DLNM) of Gasparrini, Armstrong & Kenward (2010) solves this with a cross-basis: the outer product of two spline bases — one on the exposure dimension (captures the U/J-shaped curve: risk rising with both cold and heat) and one on the lag dimension (captures how the effect is distributed over the days). The R implementation is the dlnm package (Gasparrini, 2011), on top of which climasus4r builds sus_mod_dlnm().

The fit follows the good practices for time-series regression in environmental epidemiology systematized by Bhaskaran et al. (2013): a log-linear quasi-Poisson model (robust to overdispersion), control for long-term trend and seasonality via a natural spline of time, and adjustment for day of week. The attributable fraction decomposes the total burden of events into heat and cold components (Gasparrini & Armstrong, 2013).

Guiding case. We investigate temperature and health outcomes in older adults (60+) in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region, 2014–2019 (respiratory J00–J99 and cardiovascular I00–I99). Here we join the daily death series (caso_serie.rds, Tutorial 4) with the temperature from INMET station A701 (São Paulo – Mirante de Santana), already aligned (caso_clima_estacao.rds, Tutorial 7), build the distributed-lag structure, and fit the DLNM to estimate the exposure-response curve and the burden attributable to heat and cold.

Data used

Input Source Content Role
dados/caso_serie.rds Tutorial 4 Daily death series (older adults 60+) Outcome n_obitos
dados/caso_clima_estacao.rds Tutorial 7 Daily temperature from station A701 Exposure tair_dry_bulb_c

The two series are joined by date. The exposure is then expanded into distributed-lag columns (tair_dry_bulb_c_lag0, …, tair_dry_bulb_c_lag21), a structure that in a full workflow is produced by sus_climate_aggregate(temporal_strategy = "distributed_lag", lag_days = 21). The script guards this stage with requireNamespace()/tryCatch() and, if the inputs are missing, generates a minimal, realistic synthetic series (with a V-shaped temperature-mortality signal) purely for illustration.

Full pipeline

The blocks below reproduce what scripts/tutorial_09_modelagem.R executes.

library(climasus4r)

Building the DLNM input (distributed lags)

sus_mod_dlnm() expects a climasus_df at stage "climate" and type "distributed_lag", with the date column, the outcome, and the {variable}_lag0 … _lagL columns. In a real workflow this comes from sus_climate_aggregate():

df_dl <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  health_data       = caso_serie,          # health series (from Tutorial 4)
  climate_data      = caso_clima_estacao,  # aligned temperature (from Tutorial 7)
  climate_var       = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  temporal_strategy = "distributed_lag",
  lag_days          = 21,
  lang              = "pt"
)

Fitting the DLNM (sus_mod_dlnm)

Cross-basis with exposure on a natural spline with 4 degrees of freedom (captures the U/J heat+cold shape) and lag on a natural spline with 3 degrees (smooth decay), quasi-Poisson family, and automatic seasonal control (dof_per_year = 6, recommended for subtropical Brazil):

fit <- sus_mod_dlnm(
  df           = df_dl,
  outcome_col  = "n_obitos",
  climate_col  = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  lag_max      = 21,
  argvar       = list(fun = "ns", df = 4),  # exposure dimension
  arglag       = list(fun = "ns", df = 3),  # lag dimension
  family       = "quasipoisson",
  dof_per_year = 6L,                        # df/year for seasonality
  lang         = "pt"
)

print(fit)
fit$exposure_response   # cumulative RR on the percentile grid
fit$lag_response        # RR by lag at the 75th percentile
fit$diagnostics$disp_ratio

Attributable fraction from heat and cold (sus_mod_af)

From the fitted DLNM, we decompose the total burden of deaths into heat (above the comfort threshold) and cold (below it) components, with confidence intervals from Monte Carlo simulation:

af <- sus_mod_af(
  fit  = fit,
  by   = "month",   # optional monthly breakdown
  nsim = 200L,      # use 5000L for publication-quality results
  lang = "pt"
)

print(af)
af$total        # total AF/AN, heat and cold
af$by_period    # monthly breakdown

Visualizing (sus_mod_plot_dlnm)

The package offers ready-made scientific visualizations — exposure-response curve, lag-response, 3-D surface, contour, lag slices, distribution, and time series:

sus_mod_plot_dlnm(fit, type = "overall", lang = "pt")  # exposure-response
sus_mod_plot_dlnm(fit, type = "contour", lang = "pt")  # log(RR) surface
sus_mod_plot_dlnm(fit, type = "lag",     lang = "pt")  # lag-response

Function characteristics

sus_mod_dlnm() — Distributed Lag Non-linear Model

Argument Essential? Description
df yes climasus_df at stage = "climate", type = "distributed_lag"
outcome_col yes Daily count column (e.g., "n_obitos")
climate_col optional Exposure base without the _lagN suffix; NULL auto-detects
lag_max optional Maximum lag; NULL detects it from the largest _lagN present
argvar optional Exposure basis (e.g., list(fun = "ns", df = 4))
arglag optional Lag basis (e.g., list(fun = "ns", df = 3))
family optional "quasipoisson" (default), "poisson", "negbin" (→ quasi)
ns_df / dof_per_year optional Degrees of freedom of the time spline (seasonality)
ref_value optional Reference value (RR = 1); NULL uses the median
covariates optional Additional linear confounders (humidity, etc.)

Returns: a climasus_dlnm object with $model (GLM), $crossbasis, $pred (crosspred on a 100-point grid), $exposure_response, $lag_response, $models (one-line summary), $data_daily, and $diagnostics (dispersion, Ljung-Box autocorrelation, AIC).

sus_mod_af() — Attributable Fraction and Number

Argument Description
fit climasus_dlnm object from sus_mod_dlnm()
threshold Threshold separating heat (above) and cold (below); NULL uses ref_value
pred_at Percentiles of the ranges (default c(0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99))
by Temporal breakdown: "month", "year", "season", or NULL
nsim Monte Carlo simulations for the CI (default 1000L)
alpha Significance level (default 0.05 → 95% CI)

Returns: climasus_af with $total (total/heat/cold), $by_quantile, $by_period, $daily, and $custom.

sus_mod_its() — Interrupted Time Series

Segmented Poisson regression for the effect of interventions (policies, extreme events, pandemics) on a count series (Bernal et al., 2017).

Argument Description
data climasus_df (aggregate/climate) or data.frame with date + count
outcome_col / date_col Outcome and date columns
interruption_dates One or more intervention dates (within the range)
harmonics Sinusoidal pairs for seasonality (default 2L)
family "quasipoisson" (default) or "poisson"
counterfactual Projects the pre-intervention trend (default TRUE)

Returns: climasus_its with $effects (level and trend change), $counterfactual, and $segments.

sus_mod_casecrossover() — Time-Stratified Case-Crossover

Each time stratum (month/week) acts as its own control, removing trend and seasonality by design (Maclure, 1991; Armstrong et al., 2014).

Argument Description
data climasus_df or data.frame with date, outcome, and exposure
outcome_col / exposure_col Outcome and exposure (no auto-detection)
stratum "month" (default), "week", or an existing column
lag Single integer lag or vector (moving average, e.g., 0:6)
method "conditional_poisson" (default) or "clogit"
family "quasipoisson" (default) or "poisson"

Returns: climasus_casecrossover with $or_table (OR, CI, p) and $diagnostics.

sus_mod_pool() — Multi-City Meta-Analysis

Combines DLNM estimates from several cities via multivariate meta-analysis (REML via mvmeta), producing a pooled curve, heterogeneity (Q, I²), and per-city BLUPs (Gasparrini et al., 2012).

Argument Description
fits Named list of climasus_dlnm objects (same cross-basis)
method "reml" (default), "ml", or "fixed"
blup Computes per-city BLUP predictions (default TRUE)
pred_at Percentiles of the pooled table

Returns: climasus_pool with $exposure_response, $lag_response, $heterogeneity, $city_table, and $blup_preds.

Statistical formulation

The DLNM models the daily count YtY_t as quasi-Poisson with mean μt\mu_t. The log-linear predictor combines the cross-basis cb(xt,ℓ;β)\mathrm{cb}(x_t, \ell; \beta) — the effect of the exposure history xt,xt−1,…,xt−Lx_{t}, x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_{t-L} — with control for seasonality (natural spline of time) and day of week (DOW):

log⁡𝔼(Yt)=α+cb(xt,ℓ;β)+ns(tempo)+DOW. \log\,\mathbb{E}(Y_t) \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \mathrm{cb}(x_t,\,\ell;\,\beta) \;+\; \mathrm{ns}(\text{tempo}) \;+\; \mathrm{DOW}.

The cross-basis is the outer product of a basis on exposure (argvar) and a basis on lag (arglag). The cumulative effect across all lags, at exposure level xx relative to the reference x0x_0, is

RRcum(x)=exp⁡{∑ℓ=0L[f(x,ℓ)−f(x0,ℓ)]}. RR_{\text{cum}}(x) \;=\; \exp\!\left\{ \sum_{\ell=0}^{L} \big[ f(x,\ell) - f(x_0,\ell) \big] \right\}.

The cumulative attributable fraction associated with the exposure history follows the form (Gasparrini & Armstrong, 2013):

AF=1−exp⁡(−∑ℓ=0Lβℓxt−ℓ),ANt=Yt(1−1RRt), AF \;=\; 1 - \exp\!\left( -\sum_{\ell=0}^{L} \beta_\ell\, x_{t-\ell} \right), \qquad AN_t \;=\; Y_t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{RR_t} \right),

with the daily attributable number ANtAN_t summed over the period and the CI obtained by Monte Carlo simulation of the cross-basis coefficients.

Modeling decisions

  • Overdispersion. Death counts typically have variance greater than the mean (ϕ̂>1\hat\phi > 1). The quasi-Poisson family inflates the standard error by ϕ̂\sqrt{\hat\phi} and is recommended when the dispersion ratio exceeds ~1.5 (Armstrong, 2006). The negative binomial (NB) alternative is incompatible with dlnm::crossbasis(), and climasus4r redirects it to quasi-Poisson.
  • Choice of knots and lags. For exposure, ns with 4 df captures the U/J shape (cold + heat) well; 3 df is more conservative, 5 df requires a large N. For lag, ns with 3 df models the smooth decay typical of the temperature-mortality relationship; a maximum lag of 21 days covers the delayed, prolonged effect of cold (Gasparrini, 2011).
  • Seasonality. The natural spline of time absorbs long-term trend and the annual cycle that confound the association. A value of ~dof_per_year = 4 is recommended for 1–2 years and 6–8 for subtropical Brazil and diseases with strong seasonality (Bhaskaran et al., 2013). Underfitting leaves residual autocorrelation (Ljung-Box test in $diagnostics); overfitting consumes the signal.

Illustrated results

Figure 1. DLNM response surface: log(RR) of deaths in older adults as a function of temperature (y-axis) and lag day (x-axis). Orange tones indicate increased risk (heat, short lags); green tones, reduced risk. The two-dimensional structure reveals when, after each exposure level, the effect manifests.

Figure 2. Cumulative exposure-response curve (RR and 95% CI) summed over all lags, centered on the median temperature (reference, RR = 1). The U/J shape — rising risk with both cold and heat — is the classic signature of the temperature-mortality relationship.

Figure 3. Lag-response curve at the 75th percentile of exposure: lag-specific RR between temperature and death. It allows distinguishing the acute effect (short lags) from the delayed, prolonged effect (long lags).

Figure 4. Attributable fraction of deaths (%) decomposed into total, heat, and cold, with 95% Monte Carlo CI. In subtropical climates the cold fraction tends to exceed the heat fraction, reflecting the prolonged effect of low temperatures on older adults.
